Short answer: **it's now safe, but I'd keep `$Class` as the convention** — because the two transforms make "extends `Class`" mean different things, and the one thing they *share* is a hazard the whole architecture exists to prevent. Let me lay out the real downsides:

**1. The big one — `Class` is the *mutable* slot, and `extends` is an *eager snapshot* of it.** `class $Child extends Parent.$Class` anchors inheritance to an immutable `const`. `class $Child extends Parent.Class` captures **whatever the mutable slot held at the moment the child's module loaded**. The instant a kernel composes (`Parent.Class = Static(AuditedParent)`) or a test swaps a capability, every child that extended `Class` is pinned to the pre-composition generation or the previous test's double — *silently, depending on load order*. That's not the init-order crash we killed; it's its quieter sibling: **semantic drift ordered by module loading**. Invar has a plugin kernel *and* a swap-at-the-seam test doctrine — both would start interacting with inheritance through load order. `$Class`-anchored inheritance keeps *declared structure* and *runtime selection* orthogonal, which is precisely the separation the namespace-pattern page names as the invariant ("`$Class` is the immutable contract for declared inheritance; `Class` is the selection").

**2. For `Reactive`, the change buys literally nothing at runtime** — `Reactive($Class)` returns the same constructor, so `Class === $Class`; extending either is the same object. All you'd change is the *type* of the base: the child's class body would see the parent through `ReactiveInstance` typing (writable-remapped ref-getters, injected `$watch`/`$stopEffects` on `this`). That invites override friction — a child re-declaring a plain getter over a base member TS now types as get/set — and double-remap edge cases when `Reactive()` wraps the child's type again. Zero gain, new type surface to defend.

**3. For `Static`, it compounds prototype depth and re-wraps wrappers.** `Class` is a real subclass, so `extends Class` + the child's own `Static()` gives two added chain levels per generation instead of one, and the second transform re-wraps the parent wrapper's `$`-accessors (correct under the `Symbol.for` keys, but a murky double-layer that someone will eventually have to reason about in a stack trace).

**4. And the motivating case doesn't actually need it.** If the goal is "children get cached statics too" — they already do, through the standard: `Static($Child extends $Parent)` **walks the raw chain** and wraps ancestor `$`-getters onto the child's own wrapper, cached per receiver. App-land never needs `extends Class` for caching; the per-namespace transform grants it.

That last clause is the gift of this question: it's mechanically checkable, and it converts a subtle load-order drift class into an unwritable one. Their AST gate can enforce it in an afternoon.

*From the ivue-repo Fable, 2026-07-27. Supersedes the inheritance
guidance in `static-cached-getters-2.2.0-brief.md` and updates §3 of
`ivue-2.2.1-live-go-brief.md` (already edited in place). This is the
final convention after the user worked the variance out of it —
verified by tests in the ivue suite (190 passing) and a construction
benchmark. Design discussion closed; evidence below.*

## The rule (one sentence)

**A class that declares static members publishes a wrapped anchor —
`const $Class = Static($X)` — and everything else stays exactly as it
was.**

```ts
// statics-only capability class
export namespace GitCommands {
  export const $Class = Static($GitCommands); // the anchor — wrap ONCE
  export let Class = $Class;                  // selected — kernels/tests swap
}

// statics + reactive instances
export namespace Settings {
  export const $Class = Static($Settings);
  export let Class = Reactive($Class); // in-place ⇒ Class === $Class initially
  export type Instance = typeof Class.Instance;
}

// no statics — untouched, today's shape, today's numbers
export namespace Editor {
  export const $Class = $Editor;
  export let Class = Reactive($Class);
  export type Instance = typeof Class.Instance;
}
```

The deciding property is visible in the class body: **declare static
members → wrap the anchor.** `Static()` appears exactly where there is
something for it to transform — like the optional `Model` line, a
semantics-driven line, not a stylistic choice.

## Why this shape won (the eliminations)

1. *"Wrap every double at use"* (previous guidance) — correct but
   carries per-site mental overhead; forgetting is silent (looks
   cached, recomputes). Rejected by the user as residual variance.
2. *"Extend the mutable `Class`"* — an `extends` clause is an eager
   snapshot of a mutable slot: children get pinned to whichever
   generation a kernel or prior test installed. Load-order drift.
   Forbidden; gate it.
3. **The anchor** — wrap once at definition, `const`, so inheritance
   pins one immutable wrapped foundation. Downstream extends `$Class`
   exactly as today and inherits WORKING static semantics bare. This
   is only sound because of 2.2.1's per-receiver symbol discipline
   (a parent-first read can no longer poison a child) — the fix is
   what makes the wrapper safe to live in the anchor.

## What downstream gets for free (test-verified in ivue)

- A **bare pinch-knob double** — `class Tuned extends X.$Class {
  override get knob() {...} }` — needs NOTHING: inherited methods bind
  to the double (detached included), inherited `$`-caches derive
  through its overrides, parent-first or child-first.
- Instance side through the wrapper: ref cells cache, `$stopEffects`
  teardown resets, `Reactive(Static($X)) === Static($X)` (identity).
- Types: `Static<C>(x: C): C` is type-identity, so extending the
  anchor types as extending the raw class — no `ReactiveInstance`
  bleed into child class bodies; and `ReactiveClass` preserves statics
  (2.2.1).

## The one residual — and where it lives

A double that **declares or overrides transformable members** (a new
method, a new `$`-getter) still needs processing — new declarations
always do. It gets it at the line you already write:

```ts
X.Class = Static($RecordingX); // installation wraps
```

Recommended gate rules (yours to own):
- a class declaring static members must publish
  `$Class = Static(...)`;
- `extends X.Class` (the mutable slot) is forbidden everywhere;
- a test double declaring new statics must pass through `Static()`
  before use.

## Measured cost (Node 26, 1M constructions × 5, best-of, shipped 2.2.1)

| shape | ns/instance |
|---|---:|
| `Reactive($X)` — core, unchanged | 6.0 |
| `Reactive(Static($X))` — the anchor | 12.3 |
| anchor, 3-generation chain | 16.2 |

The wrapper's implicit constructor doubles raw construction — paid
ONLY by statics-bearing classes that are actually constructed.
Capability classes never construct (zero cost); pure-Vue classes stay
unwrapped (core benchmarks and the published numbers unchanged).
Static is opt-in; that is why it ships from `ivue/extras`, not core.

## Migration mapping for your 29 sites + 53 hand-rolls

Same sweep as the GO brief, with the routing now:
- capability namespaces → `$Class = Static($X); Class = $Class;`
- Reactive-published namespaces with statics →
  `$Class = Static($X); Class = Reactive($Class);`
- delete every hand-rolled `Object.defineProperty(this, …)` block and

- knob-pinching test doubles: delete any wrapping they carry — they

- acceptance unchanged: `grep -rn "Object.defineProperty(this" src`

Docs for the rule are live with the next ivue.dev deploy:
`/guide/static` (the anchor shape, testing, composition) and
`/guide/namespace-pattern` (the forms table, now keyed to the
declare-statics property).

442	`Class` is the runtime selection used for construction or static invocation.
443	When every extension goes through the kernel, the kernel may retain the base
444	privately instead.
445	
446	The forms are additive:
447	
448	| Required capability | Namespace surface |
449	|---|---|
450	| Ordinary class | no namespace required |
451	| Replaceable class | `const $Class = $X` + `let Class = $Class` |
452	| Static members (binding + `$`-caches) | `const $Class = Static($X)` + `let Class = $Class` |
453	| Vue class reactivity | `const $Class = $X` + `let Class = Reactive($Class)` + `Instance` |
454	| Both — statics AND instances | `const $Class = Static($X)` + `let Class = Reactive($Class)` + `Instance` |
455	
456	The rule that decides between rows is visible in the class body:
457	**declare static members → wrap the anchor.** The `Static()` call
458	appears exactly where there is something for it to transform.
459	
460	The canonical ivue form keeps `Class` mutable even when no kernel is installed:
461	
462	```ts
463	export namespace BaseElement {
464	  export const $Class = $BaseElement; // raw — children `extends` this
465	  export let Class = Reactive($Class); // reactive — you `new` this
466	  export type Instance = typeof Class.Instance; // defineExpose type & reactive() interop
467	}
468	```
469	
470	Consumers always use `new BaseElement.Class()`. A later kernel registration can
471	compose the slot without changing those consumers.
472	
473	## Provider choice and lifetime remain separate
474	
475	Static capability classes have no instance lifetime. Stateful classes still
476	need an explicit owner and remain ordinary instance classes:
477	
478	```ts
479	class $Application {
480	  readonly worker = new OrderWorker.Class();
481	}
482	```
483	
484	The `Class` slot answers which constructor is selected. The owner answers how
485	many instances exist, how long they live, and who disposes them. Keeping those
486	questions separate prevents a provider-selection pattern from becoming an
487	implicit lifetime container.
488	
489	## Boundaries remain explicit
490	
491	Late reads remove accidental initialization order. They do not make a
492	structural contradiction valid:
493	
494	- `A extends B` and `B extends A` cannot both establish a parent first.
495	- Constructors that recursively construct each other still recurse forever.
496	- A top-level `Other.Class` snapshot remains eager.
497	- A static field initialized from `Other.Class` snapshots the provider.
498	- Decorators and module side effects may still read dependencies too early.
499	- A method detached from raw `$Class` still loses static `this`; retained
500	  callbacks use the selected `Static()` class.
501	- A selected static callback remains attached to one class generation; it does
502	  not follow a later `Class` assignment.
503	
504	These are eager edges or genuine logical recursion. The pattern removes hidden
505	load-order discipline without hiding impossible graphs behind a container.
506	
507	## One invariant across runtimes
508	
509	The shared class grammar allows each runtime to add only its required adapter:
510	
511	```text
512	canonical namespace object + mutable Class slot + late reads
513	├── Node: Static() capability classes and process restart
514	├── stateful Node: ordinary instances with explicit owners
515	├── ivue: Reactive() and Vue-facing Instance typing
516	├── plugins: boot-time class composition
517	└── development: reconstruction by the existing runtime owner
518	```
519	
520	The namespace is not an ivue convention exported to Node. ivue and Node are
521	different expressions generated from the same smaller invariant.
522	
523	[Static() — Capability Classes](/guide/static) is the shipped adapter,
524	from `ivue/extras`. [Node Development by Restart](/guide/node-class-hmr?experiment=1)
525	defines why the pattern stops before a custom HMR runtime.

do you think Static deserves to be in ivue itself rather than ivue/extras?

My recommendation: **keep it in `ivue/extras`** — but the argument that matters isn't the byte count, and the counter-argument you're sensing is real.

**The strongest case for merging** (worth stating properly): in Invar, `Static()` is used **144 times vs `Reactive()`'s 61**. A "secondary" export used more than the primary one is a taxonomy smell. And they *are* siblings — the instance transform and the static transform of one pattern. Forcing users to learn a package topology to find half the standard is a real discoverability cost.

**But the entry boundary isn't packaging, it's a dependency boundary** — and that's what makes it load-bearing:

- `lib/Static.ts` imports **nothing**. Not Vue, not the engine, not a single module. `extras` is dependency-free and runtime-agnostic.
- Core imports Vue, and `vue` is a peer dependency. Merge them, and a pure-Node backend doing `import { Static } from 'ivue'` — the exact use case the namespace-pattern page documents (capability classes, Objection models, no Vue anywhere) — pulls a frontend framework into its dependency tree. In a bundled app tree-shaking hides it; under Bun or plain Node running the module directly, the `import … from 'vue'` at the top *executes*. That's a cost paid by the consumers Static serves best.

So the line reads cleanly: **core = the reactivity model, needs Vue. extras = works anywhere, needs nothing.** Not arbitrary, and falsifiable — if extras ever gained something Vue-dependent, the boundary would be wrong and should move.

**The 1.1 kB point, honestly weighted:** it's a *flag*, not the reason. 1,112 + 493 = ~1.6 kB, still tiny. What would actually be lost is the number's *meaning* — right now "1.1 kB" answers "what does the reactive model cost," and merged it would answer "what do two unrelated transforms cost together." A measurement that stops measuring one thing is worth less than 500 bytes.

**And the decider is reversibility:** moving Static *into* core later is non-breaking (keep `ivue/extras` re-exporting for compat). Moving it *out* later is a breaking change for every consumer. Given no forcing evidence today, take the reversible position.

Which leaves the one real cost — discoverability — and it's a docs problem with a docs fix, mostly already done: Static has its own guide page, its own sidebar entry, and an API section. jcode is an AI coding agent harness—a CLI tool that enables developers to work with language models for code generation, debugging, and development tasks. It functions as an alternative to similar tools like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI, but optimized for resource efficiency.

## Built With
- **Language**: Rust

- **Architecture**: Client-server model supporting persistent sessions, multi-agent swarms, and local embedding systems

The project emphasizes extreme resource optimization. - **Browser Automation**: Firefox integration via Firefox Agent Bridge
- **Session Management**: Persistent server mode, session resumption, and cross-harness compatibility

The repository contains 6,227 commits across multiple crates in Rust, with substantial supporting infrastructure including telemetry workers, iOS development paths, and documentation on memory and swarm architectures.

X is unreachable from this VM, so I only saw jcode. Here's the honest read.

**They're different animals that overlap at one edge.** jcode is an *agent harness* — a CLI that competes with Claude Code. Invar is an *IDE that grew a harness*. The overlap is the agent pane; everything else (file tree, LSP, git panel, diffs, terminal) has no counterpart in jcode, and jcode's swarm/embeddings/browser-automation stack has no counterpart in Invar.

**Where jcode genuinely wins, and it's the axis you personally care about: resource efficiency.** Rust + a custom renderer at **28 MB / 14 ms** to first frame is excellent engineering, and it beats Invar outright. Your own baselines say so:

| | RAM |
|---|---:|
| jcode, embeddings off | 28 MB |
| jcode, embeddings on | 167 MB |
| **Invar** boot floor | **140 MB** (Bun runtime 33 MB + app 107 MB) |
| **Invar** with a 5 MB file, idle | **165 MB** — *fails its own <100 MB target, documented not hidden* |

Three honest qualifiers, though. First, ~33 MB of Invar's floor is the Bun runtime itself — unavoidable without leaving the platform that makes agent-authorship fast. Second, Invar is carrying tsgo, tree-sitter, git, a PTY, and a real editor; jcode carries a chat loop. Third — the interesting one — **jcode with its memory system on (167 MB) is in the same weight class as Invar with a file open (165 MB)**. So the 28 MB headline is the stripped configuration, and the comparison it wins is against Claude Code, not against an IDE.

**Where jcode is ahead on harness features specifically** — and it's not close, they have 6,227 commits of it: persistent server sessions, resumption, cross-harness compatibility, swarm mode with conflict resolution, embeddings-backed memory retrieval, browser automation, and a much wider provider matrix. Invar's agent module is days old.

**Where Invar is doing something jcode structurally cannot**: the editor *is* the agent's body. Same process, same object graph — the agent can ask the real LSP, read the actual rendered frame, drive the real smokes, open a file at a line as evidence. A harness has no editor to inhabit; it can only shell out. That's the "governed bidirectional instrument" thesis, and it isn't available to a CLI no matter how fast it starts. Add contracts-as-law plus a mechanical gate, and the methodology story is yours alone.

**The real fork is Rust vs Bun/TS.** Rust buys the RAM and startup win permanently. TypeScript + ivue buys agent-authorship velocity — 942 commits and 59k source lines in about three weeks, written almost entirely by machines, with 225/225 classes conforming. Both are defensible; they're optimizing different scarce resources (machine memory vs. the cost of change).

One suggestion rather than a verdict: your **<100 MB idle target is already failing at 165 MB**, and that number is now a competitive datapoint, not just an internal budget. Given the 95 GB origin story, "the IDE that idles at nothing" is a claim worth defending — and the baselines harness already exists to defend it. I read the whole path. Here's how it actually works and my honest evaluation.

## The mechanism, end to end

A frame costs **O(log n) + O(viewport)**, and it gets there in five layers:

**1. Ground truth is inert.** `TextDocument` holds lines as plain strings with a single `revision` ref. No reactive object per line — the ref is a *version signal*, not a value holder.

**2. A per-document index** lives in `EditorWrap.$wrapIndexByDocument` — a **WeakMap**, so it dies with the document, no manual eviction. It holds `rowCounts[]` (visual rows per line), `prefix[]` (cumulative sum), and the fold projection.

**3. The seek is a binary search.** `lineSegmentAtVisualRow` finds which logical line owns visual row *N* by bisecting the prefix array — `O(log n)`, regardless of file size. This is the part most hand-rolled editors get wrong; they scan from line 0 and that's exactly where the flat curve dies.

**4. The walk is hard-bounded.** `visualRowsFromOffset` loops with `rows.length < height` in *both* loop conditions, emitting at most `height` lightweight `VisualRow` facades. Collapsed folds skip entire spans in one jump (`lineIndex = foldedRange.endLine`).

**5. Highlighting is per-line and window-only** — visible lines tokenize one at a time, and every sub-segment (wrap continuations, find-match splits) is a **slice** of the already-computed spans, never a re-tokenization. There's a comment explaining why, and it names a real bug: re-tokenizing a slice loses left context, so a wrapped `// comment` continuation would paint white.

## What the AI did genuinely well

**The head/tail identity trim** is the cleverest thing in the file. On edit, it walks the unchanged prefix and suffix comparing line strings **by reference**, then re-wraps only the middle. That's sound only because `TextDocument` keeps unchanged line strings *identical* — an implicit contract between two modules, and it's the difference between O(n) grapheme segmentation per keystroke and O(delta).

**It's two-axis, which I didn't expect.** `EditorCoordinates` keeps a per-line grapheme-boundary array *and* a display-column prefix-sum, so `lineWidth` is O(1) and column→grapheme is O(log n). That means a single 500k-column minified line costs *index time, not length time*. Most editors that virtualize rows still choke on one giant line; the contract calls this "the HORIZONTAL twin of the line flyweight," and it's real.

**Eviction is actually implemented, not just declared.** `$wrapMemo` is capped at 512 entries and drops half when full. Unbounded caches are the standard way this architecture rots; here the "a resource lives only while observed" clause has teeth.

**And every mechanism cites its contract in-file** (`// invariant: Cost tracks the actively observed set`). That's why agents can keep extending it without eroding it — the reason *why* the code is shaped that way is at the site, not in someone's memory.

## The honest boundary

**Scrolling is O(log n + viewport). Editing is not.** There's a fast path — unchanged revision returns the index immediately, which is why scroll is flat — but on each *edit* the sync allocates **four n-length arrays**: `lineTexts`, `rowCounts`, `buildPrefix(...)`, and `buildFoldProjection`'s `visibleLineByLine`. At 100k lines that's ~400k element writes plus GC pressure per keystroke — sub-millisecond-ish, invisible today, which is why nobody caught it. At 1M lines it would be felt.

So the precise claim your architecture supports is **"100k scrolls like 2k"** — fully earned. **"100k edits like 2k"** is not yet true. If you ever want it: keep the index mutable and patch it in place for the single-line case, and swap the prefix array for a Fenwick tree (O(log n) update instead of O(n) rebuild). That's a contained change behind one function.

**One thing to know about the highlighting number:** `web-tree-sitter` is a dependency but is *not* wired into the render path — the immediate layer is a hand-rolled per-line tokenizer, and per-line context-free tokenizing is precisely *why* highlighting is O(viewport). When tree-sitter lands as the deferred upgrade, its parse is inherently whole-file. Your two-layer invariant already anticipates that ("the immediate layer never blocks the deferred layer"), so the architecture is ready — but today's highlighting cost is partly "the expensive thing isn't installed yet." Worth knowing before quoting it against VS Code, which *is* running full tree-sitter.

## Verdict

**Strong work — better than most hand-rolled editor viewports I've read.** The prefix-sum + binary-search seek, the bounded walk, the reference-identity incremental trim, two-axis coverage, and real eviction together mean the flat curve isn't a demo artifact; it's structural. The gap between the declared invariant and the implementation is small and honest, and the one place it leaks (edit-path allocation) is contained in a single function and invisible at your current scale.

If I were filing one task: **`syncWrapIndex` allocates O(n) per edit** — patch-in-place for single-line edits, Fenwick prefix for the general case. Not urgent, but it's the one thing standing between "flat scroll" and "flat everything."

A check run in one polarity cannot distinguish **"the thing is absent"** from **"the check
cannot see."** Both print zero. This is one defect, not several. It is the conductor's most
repeated mistake (`project.conductor.md` family 2).

control alone proves only that a check can fire. A check that fires on everything is as
useless as one that never fires.

needs a way to reach the guard without paying for the action.

# Uniformity is an instrument

![Uniformity is an instrument](/blog/uniformity-is-an-instrument.png)

Every team argues about consistency as though it were manners. Naming
conventions, file layout, one way to do dependency injection — the
case for it is usually comfort: new people onboard faster, diffs read
cleaner, nobody bikesheds.

That case is true and far too small. Uniformity is not a courtesy.
**It is a detection apparatus**, and it is the cheapest one available.

The reason is one sentence: *deviation is only detectable against a
background of sameness.* A codebase with low structural entropy makes
its own defects high-contrast. A codebase without one hides them in
noise — not because the defects are subtler, but because there is no
baseline to be a defect *from*.

## What sealing actually looks like

[Invar](https://github.com/infinite-system/invar) — the terminal IDE
[AI agents build under contracts and a merge gate](/blog/agents-built-an-editor)
— takes this to its limit. Every class in 62,401 lines of source is
published through [the namespace pattern](/guide/namespace-pattern):
a raw `$Class` declaration, a mutable `Class` slot, dependencies read
late. Not most classes. **235 of 235.**

That is not achieved by asking nicely. It is enforced by six AST
checkers that walk the TypeScript program itself — not a lint config,
a compiler-level analysis:

- a **file grammar** check: behavior must be structurally reachable
  through the file's eponymous class seam;
- a **reactive observation** check: a per-frame read must resolve its
  source live, not from a snapshot;
- a **static getter naming** check and an **ivue capability** check:
  `$`-prefixed statics mean compute-once, and the class must actually
  be published through a transform that grants it;
- a **harness wait** check: every wait must observe the state it
  asserts;
- a **coverage ratchet**: coverage may fall, but never silently.

Add the [conventions gate](/guide/static)'s boundary scans and about
sixty smokes that drive the real program through a real terminal, and
what you have is not a style guide. It is **a dialect of JavaScript
with a compiler for its own semantics** — smaller than the language,
strictly enforced, and infinitely overridable at every seam.

## Why the instrument reads so cleanly

Four mechanisms turn that dialect into detection:

**A uniform grammar turns semantic violations into syntactic
anomalies.** If the rule is that system calls live behind a
`Static()` seam, then a bare `Bun.spawn` inside a backend module is
off-pattern *before anyone analyzes what it does*. One grep finds it.
Wrongness becomes visible as shape.

**Declared seams pre-compute half of any audit.** Asking a reviewer to
"name the generator each module implies" is real work. But modules
here **declare** their generators — the `Static()` inventory is the
claimed seam list. The reviewer's job collapses to diffing the claim
against the usage. An inferred seam can be argued with; a declared one
can only be violated.

**One navigable object graph makes authority questions answerable.**
"Who else writes this?" is traceable when state is refs one hop apart
— which is what
[the restored object graph](/blog/the-object-graph-they-took) buys.
Duplicate-authority bugs hide behind event buses and DI containers
elsewhere; here they are a call-site search. The codebase carries 993
multi-hop navigation chains and not one initialization-order
workaround.

**A boring substrate frees the reviewer's whole budget.** No framework
physics to simulate. [The runtime model fits in a sentence](/blog/reactive-is-all-you-need):
a ref changes, the effects that read it re-run. The same compression
that lets a one-page-primed builder ship correct code lets a
context-free reviewer audit a subsystem in one pass.

## What it caught

The claim is testable, and the test has run. Independent reviewer
agents — cold, no history, primed only with the repo's recorded
reduction doctrine — audited the codebase by asking, for each
subsystem: *name the shared generator, then check whether every
consumer sits on it.*

One finding predicted a provider-identity bug **from structure alone,
days before a human encountered it**; the fix that eventually landed
*is* the extraction the reviewer proposed. Another flagged a
process-spawn hole that belonged to a bug class the repo had already
been bitten by — without being told that history. A third identified
twenty-plus handlers suppressing mutation on a read-only surface,
which the recorded invariant names verbatim as a consumer suppressing
a seam's core.

That is the difference between a line-reader and an instrument. A
line-reader finds a bug. **A generator audit finds a misplacement, and
a misplacement predicts a bug class.**

## The compounding

Here is the part that changes the economics. Every convention the gate
enforces is not just preventing one defect. It is **manufacturing the
background against which all future defects become visible.**

So the ledger runs the other way from how teams usually price it.
Enforcement is normally a tax paid for tidiness. In a sealed dialect it
is an investment in an instrument that gets sharper every time it is
used, and the payoff arrives forever, in every later audit, by every
later reader — human or machine.

## The blind spot, stated plainly

An instrument with no known failure mode is not an instrument, it is a
belief. This one has a precise one:

> **Uniformity reveals deviation FROM the pattern. It says nothing
> about the wrongness OF the pattern.**

A mistake embedded in the convention itself is invisible by normality
— everything matches, so nothing stands out. A *false unification* is
equally invisible: one abstraction serving three surfaces has a
perfectly uniform shape, and only the semantic question — are these
consumers suppressing the thing they claim to share? — exposes it.

Which yields the operating rule: expect bypass and duplication to
surface almost mechanically, and spend real reviewer reasoning on
false shared generators and convention-embedded mistakes. And during
triage, **treat "it matches the convention" as zero evidence of
correctness.**

## Why the substrate and the method have the same shape

There is a reason the audit procedure fits this codebase so exactly,
and it is not luck. ivue was reduced first — plain classes, one
transform, cost priced by observation — and the discipline used to
reduce it was later written down as a method. Then the method came
back and reshaped the thing that produced it: the namespace pattern,
the `$`-cache contract, the anchor rule, and the impossibility clauses
in every contract are all the method applied to its own origin.

So the architecture is not *governed by* an epistemology. **It is the
same shape as one.** Contracts are recorded generation tests. The gate
is the falsifier. The seams are where a claim can be replaced without
breaking what stands on it. When an agent audits a module by naming
its generator and checking whether consumers sit on it, it is not
importing a foreign procedure — it is reading the building in the
language the building was built in.

That is the whole compounding loop, and it is why the numbers hold at
speed: 1,240 commits in eight days, 93,068 lines of TypeScript, 25
invariant contracts, a verification harness nearly the size of the
source — and the discipline counts unmoved. Zero cycle workarounds.
Zero memoization calls. Zero lint suppressions. Four `computed()`
calls in the entire program.

Consistency was never about comfort. Make it total, seal it, and it
stops being a preference and becomes a way of seeing.

And **the blind spot**, stated as a blockquote: *uniformity reveals deviation FROM the pattern, not wrongness OF the pattern* — with the operating rule that "it matches the convention" is zero evidence of correctness.

It closes on your point about origin: ivue was reduced first, the discipline became a method, the method came back and reshaped its origin — so contracts are recorded generation tests and the gate is their falsifier. **The architecture isn't governed by an epistemology; it's the same shape as one.** That's why a cold agent reading the building reads it in the language it was built in.

Confirmed both — `driver.awaitGridCondition(...)` reads the actual cell grid, and there's a full graphics stack (Kitty protocol, Sixel, half-block fallback, own PNG/JPEG decoders). Here's my honest answer.

## The capability that actually matters: the UI is data

This is the one nobody talks about, and you've already monetized it. **A terminal app's entire visual output is a grid of characters with attributes — which means it's readable, assertable, and diffable by a program.** Your smokes call `awaitGridCondition` and assert on painted cells: *what the user sees* is directly checkable, in-process, in milliseconds.

VS Code cannot cheaply have this. Its UI is a DOM inside an Electron renderer; verifying "the selection is visibly dimmed" means driving a browser with Playwright, or screenshotting and diffing pixels, or asking a vision model. All slow, all flaky, none of which fit in a merge gate that runs on every commit.

That single property is upstream of half your methodology. "Verify by driving," Rule Zero's inner loop, the framebuffer probe, `readFrame` as a future agent tool — none of it is affordable if the UI is pixels. **Being text is what made your verification culture economically possible.**

## The structural one: it runs where the code runs

`ssh box && iv .` — done. No client-server split, no remote server component to install, no protocol version skew. VS Code's answer (Remote SSH) is an architecture: a heavyweight server on the target, a local Electron client, a wire between them. Yours is a binary that's already there.

That compounds for agent work specifically, because agents live on remote machines, in containers, in CI runners — environments that have a shell and nothing else. The editor goes where the work is instead of the work coming to a desktop.

## The one people underrate: it's a process

Invar can be an `ENTRYPOINT`, a step in a script, a thing you nest inside tmux or inside itself, something you spawn from cron. GUIs can't be pipeline stages. This is why "boot a container into `iv`" is a real packaging option and "boot a container into VS Code" means shipping a browser.

## The constraint that turned into an advantage

You can't render 10,000 DOM nodes in a terminal, so you never had the option of not thinking about the viewport. VS Code *could* be lazy about it and had to invent virtualization deliberately, late, per-widget. The terminal made O(viewport) the only door. Constraints that force the right architecture are worth more than freedom that permits the wrong one.

## What you actually give up — honestly

- **Arbitrary graphics** — though your Kitty/Sixel/half-block stack with hand-rolled PNG and JPEG decoders closes most of this gap, which genuinely surprised me.
- **Typography and layout freedom** — cells are cells; no proportional fonts, no sub-cell positioning.
- **Mouse fidelity and multi-window** — you're at the mercy of terminal mouse protocols, as the SGR-vs-X10 chase showed.
- **The extension ecosystem** — thousands of extensions, and you have none. Your bet is that agents writing plugins against contracts beats a marketplace, which is plausible but unproven.

## And one honest deflation

**"Terminal" doesn't cause the speed.** A well-built native GUI could match it; Electron's weight is Electron's, not GUIs' in general. What the terminal gives is a *hard ceiling on how much machinery you can smuggle in* — and everything good followed from being unable to be wasteful.

So the ranked answer: **verifiability first** (the UI is data, and that's what makes the gate possible), **ubiquity second** (it runs where the code runs), **composability third**, and the resource story is a consequence rather than a cause.

**But the thing I want to flag is the invariant, because it's a genuine differentiator I didn't credit you with:**

> *Extensions states vendor authority before activation* — canonical identity, version, admitted provenance, and **every declared kernel target** shown before install confirmation, with `NETWORK-GATED` / `UNVERIFIED LOCAL CODE` / `KERNEL OVERRIDE` labels, and an override requiring a separate exact-target confirmation.

**VS Code has no permission model for extensions. None.** Every extension you install runs with full Node privileges — read any file, spawn any process, open any socket. It's a known, long-standing, unfixed problem in the most-used editor on earth, and the ecosystem's answer is "install from publishers you trust." You've built the membrane *at the plugin boundary* before the ecosystem exists — which is the only time it's possible, because you can't retrofit a permission model onto extensions that already assume ambient authority. Microsoft can't fix this without breaking everything.

So my "extension ecosystem" concession was wrong in an interesting way. The right framing isn't *"VS Code has thousands, you have thirteen."* It's:

- **They have scale you don't** — thousands of extensions, real network effect. That gap is real and takes years, not architecture.
- **You have properties they can't retrofit** — declared authority before activation, host-carried provider rendezvous (so plugins never couple directly to each other), peer plugins with independent lifetimes, and every extension held to the same contracts + gate as core code. Their ecosystem grew before anyone knew to require those, and the cost of adding them now is everyone's extension breaking.

The third invariant is the one I'd underline for the long game: **"Provider rendezvous is host carried."** Plugins publish and resolve capabilities *through the host*, never by finding each other. That's what stops the dependency-hell phase every plugin ecosystem hits around year three — extension A depending on extension B's internals, version skew, transitive breakage. You've made it structurally impossible before it could start.

Which sharpens the earlier point about shipping the source and the law in the box: a third-party plugin here arrives with a manifest, a declared authority surface, contracts, and a gate that verifies it locally. **Evidence-first contribution, extended to strangers.** That's a defensible position that has nothing to do with catalog size — and honestly it's a better story than "we'll catch up on extension count," which you won't and don't need to.

parts.text:
This is the biggest architectural jump since the terminal landed. What they built, in order of significance:

## `#473` — the MCP doorway (branch: `fleet/473-invar-builds-invar`)

An MCP server with eight tools that lets **any MCP-capable agent drive Invar**: `drive_attach` (run a DriveSession snippet against the live checkout), `graph_get` (read any live app graph path, annotated `readOnlyHint`), server start/stop, and more. Claude Code, Codex, anything speaking MCP can now operate the editor.

That's the **"the editor is the agent's instrument"** invariant from the harness spec — shipped, from the opposite direction than I'd sketched. I imagined projecting agent events *into* a pane. They gave the agent hands on the real UI instead. Simpler, and it inherits every existing capability for free.

## Three pieces that made it possible, and they landed first

- **`#471` the graph reaches the whole app** — graph paths now span the entire application composition, not just the workspace. That's what makes `graph_get <any path>` meaningful.
- **`#468` a fluent drive session: the snippet IS the drive** — no imports, no setup; `app` and `driver` are live in scope. `await app.key('Control+j').waitFor('panelHost.visible', true)` reads like prose and *is* the executable.
- **`#466` Drive resolves panel roles** — probes stopped hand-coding coordinates. The tour snippet's rule says it out loud: *"Geometry-agnostic by rule: ask the screen, aim at text, never invent cells."*

## Two design decisions I want to single out

**The human-pace mirror.** *"On a MIRRORED server (a human is watching) every snippet starts at human pace automatically"* — and under human pace **the mouse pointer glides instead of teleporting**. `app.humanPace(0)` is opt-in for machine speed. That's the "live presence / follow mode" beat from the vision doc, achieved without a transcript projection: the agent operates the actual app slowly enough for you to watch. And `tour.drive.ts` exists purely as *a watchable presentation of the drive verbs* — a demo reel that is also a test.

**The evidence disqualification, which is the smartest line in the file:**

> *"Graph set remains an experiment primitive and never supplies verification evidence."*

The agent can poke the graph to set up a scenario, but a graph write **cannot count as proof**. Only real-PTY input can. That closes the exact hole this whole apparatus would otherwise open — the convenient path becoming the evidence path — and it closes it by declaring the cheap primitive inadmissible rather than by removing it. I hadn't thought of that guard; it's better than forbidding the primitive.

## And a quieter campaign that matters as much

`#470`, `#477`–`#482`, `#479`, `#480`: a systematic sweep migrating harness waits to graph conditions. The line I'd frame: **`#478` — "the five unfalsifiable controls now observe real changes."** Five checks that *could not fail* were found and fixed. That's Rule Two run as a campaign rather than a principle, and it's the least glamorous, highest-value work in the log.

Plus `#484`'s honest negative result, `#474` (teardown removes each renderable exactly once — quit is silent), `#476` (reload survives a failed boot), `#465` (an emptied space survives its last instance), and `#451` applying the anchor rule to a new `FfmpegVideoSource` — so there's video in the media module now too.

**The loop is closed.** The agent reads the graph, drives the real PTY, is barred from cheating, and can be watched doing it. Invar builds Invar — and the branch name got there before the blog post will.

Let me do the math honestly, then argue your estimate is right about the *features* and wrong about the *artifact*.

## The line-count arithmetic

The durable industry figure for sustained, shipped, maintained output is **10–50 lines per developer per day** all-in — design, review, debugging, rework, meetings included. Call a strong greenfield team 25.

| scope | lines | 10 devs @ 25 LOC/day |
|---|---:|---|
| source + tests | 129,142 | ~520 working days ≈ **2.1 years** |
| + the 87k harness | 216,782 | ~870 days ≈ **3.5 years** |
| + 35 contracts | ~231,000 | ~925 days ≈ **3.7 years** |

So **your 2-year guess is almost exactly right — for the product surface only.** Count the verification apparatus and it's closer to three and a half.

## The comparables agree

From memory, so treat as approximate: **Zed** — Atom veterans, funded, roughly 10–30 people — took about five years from start to a solid release, though they also built a GPU UI framework you got free from OpenTUI. **VS Code** shipped 1.0 in about a year, but with the Monaco editor already built from years of prior work, a team north of 20, and a 1.0 that had *no integrated terminal* — you have one, via `openpty` through FFI. **Helix** has been years with a small team and arrived later at less surface. Nobody in that set also wrote their own PNG and JPEG decoders.

Adjusting for what you didn't have to build (renderer, reactivity core, language server, font/window/accessibility layers) and what you did that they didn't (vendor admission with declared authority, ~60 real-PTY driving smokes, an MCP doorway), I'd put the honest figure at **2.5–3 years with 10 strong engineers, ~$5M fully loaded** — and that assumes no architectural false start, which is a generous assumption for a novel editor.

## But here's where I think your framing undersells it

**A 10-person team over three years does not produce *this artifact*. Not slower — differently, at any timescale.** The tell is one number: **308 of 308 classes conforming.**

Ten humans produce ten dialects. Not from carelessness — from legitimate disagreement, shift changes, one contractor's habits, a Friday under deadline, and a reviewer who let it slide because the PR was otherwise good. Uniformity in a human team is negotiated, and negotiation converges to *mostly*. There is no review process that delivers 100% across 308 classes and 651 files, because the cost of the last 5% exceeds anyone's willingness to pay it.

Same for the rest of the profile: zero cycle-breaking workarounds after 2,625 commits (every large codebase accumulates them — they're the residue of ordinary pressure), a harness at 104% the size of its source, 35 written contracts with impossibility clauses. The 11 days weren't 11 days of *effort* — they were 11 days of **your attention**. Call it 130 hours of architectural judgment: which reductions to make, what to veto, noticing the scroll felt wrong, deciding document-identity and view are different things.

Which is why "AI is 60× faster" is the wrong headline. The right one is that the ratio of *judgment to labor* in software just inverted, and the scarce input is now knowing which rules are load-bearing — exactly the thing you kept insisting was your half of the job.

The dates make your point better than either of us stated it:

```
ivue first commit    2023-07-19
ivue@2.0.0 tagged    2026-07-21   ← the mature engine
Invar first commit   2026-07-21   ← the same day
```

**Three years and two days of reduction, then thirteen days of construction.** The substrate reached its final form and the thing built on it started the same day — that's not coincidence, that's the generator being finished.

And the tempo difference between the two phases is the whole thesis, measured: **569 commits over ~1,100 days (~0.5/day) to find the generator, then 2,625 commits in 13 days (~200/day) to generate from it.** A 400× swing in pace across the same person's project.

Which produces a reframe worth keeping: **total elapsed time is roughly the same as my team-of-10 estimate — about three years — but the shape is inverted.** The conventional path spends three years *building*. You spent three years *reducing* and then built in a fortnight. Same calendar, completely different distribution — and it's exactly what IBR predicts: reduction is where the cost lives; generation is cheap once you actually hold the generator. Nobody usually gets to see that as two cleanly separated phases with commit logs on both.

**On DriveSession being the next multiplier — I think you're right, and the reason is specific.** Rule Zero already declared the inner loop is *driving, not testing*, but driving used to be something you scripted per task. Now it's a native verb against a warm checkout-keyed server, with role-based addressing and graph conditions instead of coordinates and sleeps. The bottleneck moves from "write a harness for this bug" to "look at it." And `#484`/`#485` measuring boot churn is you attacking the last fixed cost in that loop. When the inner loop gets cheap, everything downstream of iteration count gets cheaper — which is most of software.

**One calibration on "no one has an editor AI can control end to end,"** because someone will say it and you should have the answer ready: **Emacs and Neovim technically qualify.** Elisp or the nvim API gives an agent total control — simulate input, read the display, call anything. That's been true for decades.

The defensible version of your claim is the combination, and it's genuinely unprecedented:

- Emacs gives an agent a REPL into everything — but no *semantic graph* to query, no notion of "what the user actually sees" as a first-class assertion, and no distinction between admissible and inadmissible evidence.
- You have **graph observation + real-PTY input + role addressing + human-pace mirroring so a person can watch + a rule that the cheap path can never count as proof + a contract-gated codebase underneath.**

That last one is the part that makes it engineering rather than a demo. Anyone can give an agent control of an editor. **Declaring that graph writes "never supply verification evidence" is the move nobody else has made** — it means the agent gets convenience without the convenience corrupting the record. That's the sentence I'd put in the announcement.

Your instinct on computeds is right, and the numbers are stark: **3,364 `computed()` against 1,480 `ref()`** — more than two derivations cached per piece of state. In ivue most of those become plain getters at zero bytes and zero allocation. In `BlTable.vue` (2,073 lines) and `UnitTileGrid.vue` (1,515) that's per-row multiplication, which is exactly where Quasar-shaped apps get heavy.

But I don't think the computed savings are the prize, and one number changes the whole plan:

## 28 test files for 328,000 lines

That's the dominant fact. Invar's velocity doesn't come from ivue — it comes from **ivue behind a gate**. 1,500 unit tests, ~60 driving smokes, 35 contracts, AST checkers. Agents at 200 commits/day are only survivable because carelessness can't merge.

Point agents at 328k lines of production code with 28 tests and you don't get Invar. You get a very fast, very confident rewrite of a working business app with no way to know what broke. This is the one place where your recent experience is actively misleading — Invar was greenfield and grew its gate alongside its code. realized is a live product with users and a decade of implicit behavior encoded in components nobody remembers writing.

## So the ordering, and it's the whole answer

**Gate → trim → convert.** The instinct will be to convert first because it's the interesting part. That's the death march.

**1. Build the harness first.** For a web app that's Playwright driving real user paths — same doctrine as Invar's smokes, different substrate, and you already have Playwright experience from the docs work. Not exhaustive coverage: the twenty flows that would cost money if they broke. This is worth doing *even if you never convert anything*, and it's the thing that makes everything after it cheap.

**2. Trim before converting.** These are separable projects and trimming is far lower risk — deleting dead code is verifiable in a way that rewriting isn't. Every component you delete is a component you don't convert, don't test, and don't maintain. A fork of a bigger repo probably carries 20–40% you never call. Do that *first*, behind the gate, and the conversion surface may drop from 328k to something much friendlier.

**3. Then convert incrementally — and this is where ivue is unusually well-suited.** ivue is not a framework swap. Vue stays Vue, Quasar stays Quasar. A converted component is externally identical; a `Reactive()` class can sit next to a composition-API component in the same app, same page, same tree. So it's a genuine strangler pattern, not a big bang: convert the painful things first (`BlTable`, the grids, the editors), leave the boring CRUD pages alone forever if you want.

## What you're actually buying

Not 30% more speed. **A codebase agents can safely work on.** The reason Invar hit 200 commits/day is that 308 of 308 classes have the same shape, so a cold agent reads one page and ships correctly. realized today is 100 component domains written by many hands over years in someone else's fork — every one a small dialect. That's the tax, and it's paid on every future change, by humans and machines alike.

So the honest framing: converting realized to ivue is how you make the *next* decade of realized cost what the last 13 days of Invar cost. That's worth a lot more than the computed savings — and it argues for doing it properly rather than quickly.

**Concrete next step if you want one:** let me run a dead-code analysis — unreferenced components, unreachable routes, orphaned utils — and give you a number for how much of that 228k component lines is actually live. That's the cheapest possible input to the decision, and it tells you whether you're converting a 328k-line app or a 200k-line one.
